title: Grind half a teaspoon of peppercorns in a granite mortar to a medium-fine grind
context: Home cooks crush whole spices in a mortar and pestle just before use for fresher flavor, a step common to cuisines worldwide (Indian spice mixes, Thai curry pastes, Mexican molcajete salsas) and taught in cookbooks and cooking schools. The pestle has to be pressed down on the corns and worked round the bowl, or lifted and brought down firmly: swirled lightly it slides over whole peppercorns, and slammed down it sends them jumping out. Half a teaspoon (about 1.2 g) is a typical amount for one recipe. How fine it gets is checked the way spice grinds are sized, with sieves: pepper sold as table ground is 18-28 mesh and as fine ground 30-36 mesh, coarser than 14 mesh counts as cracked or coarse. Then the heavy pestle is put down.
setup: Positions in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases: x forward, y to the robot's left, z up from the worktop. (1) Mortar: an unpolished gray granite mortar, 12 cm across and 8.5 cm tall, 1,280 g, standing loose on the worktop (no mat, no clamp: it can slide or tip), its foot centered at x 30.0, y -8.0. Its bowl is 8 cm across at the rim and 5 cm deep, narrowing to about 6.2 cm across at the bottom. It is a standard 12 cm granite set as sold by kitchen retailers. (2) Peppercorns: 27 whole dried black peppercorns (1.2 g, about half a teaspoon, a typical amount for one recipe; Malabar grade, about 4.6 mm and 43 mg each), shaken on the 1.4 mm sieve first so nothing passes at the start, in one ring round the edge of the bowl's bottom (their centers 2.5 to 2.8 cm from the middle), the middle of the bottom clear. (3) Pestle: the set's granite pestle, 14 cm long and 330 g, with a 4 cm head and a handle 2.8 cm across. It leans in the bowl, its head on the bottom among the corns and its handle resting on the rim on the right (-y) side at about 58 degrees from upright, its top end near x 30.0, y -17.2, z 13.4. Both arms start at their ready pose. The layout is the same in every trial.
scoring: The score is the grind, read with two stacked sieves: the share by mass of the starting 27 whole corns (1.2 g), still in the mortar, that passes 1.4 mm (US No. 14) and the share that passes 0.6 mm (US No. 30). The trial scores 1.0 when 80% or more passes 1.4 mm, 20% or more passes 0.6 mm, and the pestle has been put down and let go with everything still for 1 s: the pestle rests in the bowl (the middle of its head's end inside the bowl, below the rim) or lies on the worktop (its head's end within 4 cm of the worktop and its lowest point from 3 mm below to 5 mm above it), no gripper is touching it (a release check on contact of the gripper's own shape), the mortar is upright within 10 degrees, and pestle and mortar move under 1 cm/s and turn under 10 degrees/s. A pestle left in hand can still fall. It scores 0.75 when 80% or more passes 1.4 mm and 20% or more passes 0.6 mm, whatever is done with the pestle. It scores 0.5 when 80% or more passes 1.4 mm. It scores 0.25 when 40% or more passes 1.4 mm. Otherwise it scores 0: doing nothing scores 0. The whole trial scores at most 0.25 if more than 0.12 g of pepper (about 10% of the batch, three corns) is ever outside the mortar; a mortar tipped past 60 degrees pours out and counts as outside. How the pepper was ground never changes the score. Real trial: stack the No. 14 sieve on the No. 30 sieve over a pan, tip the mortar's contents in, brushing the bowl out, shake 30 s, and weigh what reached the pan and what sits on the No. 30 sieve on a 0.01 g scale (pan and No. 30 together 0.93 g or more is 80% through 1.4 mm; the pan 0.23 g or more is 20% through 0.6 mm); brush up and weigh any pepper outside the mortar; judge the set-down on the video. Simulation: the same two shares, counted from the pepper's bodies and the masses they break into. Possible scores: 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0.
reset_notes: Each real trial starts with 27 fresh whole black peppercorns (1.2 g, Malabar grade, shaken on the 1.4 mm sieve first so nothing passes), counted into the emptied, brushed-out bowl and set round the edge of its bottom, and the pestle leaned back in as described. In simulation every trial starts with the same 27 whole corns in the same places.
fidelity: Real size and mass. Corns and cracked pieces are real bodies; only pepper under 1.4 mm is counted by mass and drawn as layers. A corn breaks when the work done on it reaches its measured rupture energy, because the force per corn while circling (10-15 N shared) is far below the 50-75 N single-squeeze crack. The fine stage's energy is not measured for pepper: it is estimated from the pieces' energy with Rittinger's law. Friction: granite on worktop 0.5, corns on granite 0.35.
